idiom_name: abstract interface + constructor-injected reference/unique_ptr, wired in main
implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses onto plain C++: the service interface is an abstract class with a virtual destructor, the consumer takes it by reference (non-owning, lifetime managed by the composition root) or by std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr (owned), and main or an application factory is the composition root. What replaces an injector is the constructor call itself: dependencies are passed explicitly, and there is no reflection or container unless you add one. Reach for a DI library only when the graph is large enough that hand wiring becomes the maintenance problem.
pitfalls: Dangling references: the injected reference must outlive the consumer - a temporary or a local destroyed too early is a silent use-after-free.
Object slicing: take the abstraction by reference or pointer, never by value.
shared_ptr everywhere hides ownership and invites cycles - prefer unique_ptr or a plain reference unless sharing is real.

variants.name: [Boost].DI compile-time injector
variants.implementation_notes: [Boost].DI is a header-only compile-time container: the injector is built as a type from binding declarations, create<T>() deduces the longest constructor and resolves each parameter recursively, and scopes (singleton per injector, unique per create) are policy types. It removes the hand-written composition root while keeping resolution at compile time - no reflection and no runtime registration cost - and its diagnostics can print a creation tree. Prefer it when the graph is deep or when test/override bindings must be swapped systematically; the price is a heavy template interface and long compile times.
pitfalls: Constructor ambiguity: with several equally long constructors Boost.DI cannot choose - mark one with BOOST_DI_INJECT or di::ctor_traits.
Template error messages for a missing binding are enormous; raise BOOST_DI_CFG_DIAGNOSTICS_LEVEL to get a creation tree.
